title: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo; Relentless, Inc. v. Department of Commerce (2024)
shortTitle: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo; Relentless, Inc. v. Department of Commerce (2024)
summary: Courts must independently determine statutory meaning under the APA. Loper Bright overruled Chevron’s ambiguity-based deference, preserved persuasive agency guidance and actual statutory delegations, and remanded the observer-payment disputes.
notes: The companion case, Relentless, Inc. v. Department of Commerce, came from the First Circuit; the challenged industry-funded monitoring program cost vessel owners an estimated $710 per day. Chief Justice Roberts wrote for a 6-3 Court (Justice Jackson took no part in Loper Bright but joined the Kagan dissent in Relentless); Justices Thomas and Gorsuch concurred; Justice Kagan dissented joined by Sotomayor and Jackson.

sections.Parties: Atlantic herring fishing businesses challenged the federal government’s requirement that they pay for some onboard observers. The National Marine Fisheries Service administered the relevant statute under authority delegated by the Secretary of Commerce. Loper Bright reached the Court from the D.C. Circuit; the companion Relentless case came from the First Circuit. The packet removes the companion case’s detailed facts and procedural discussion but identifies its materially identical role. (Printed 939–940, 961.)
sections.Material Facts:
The Magnuson-Stevens Act authorized fishery-management plans to require observers on domestic vessels to collect conservation and management data. The statute expressly imposed observer-related costs on three identified groups: foreign vessels, vessels in certain limited-access privilege programs, and vessels under the North Pacific Council’s jurisdiction. It contained no comparable payment language for the Atlantic herring fishermen at issue. NMFS had previously funded their required observers. (Printed 939.)

After an amendment proposed in 2013, NMFS adopted a rule allowing industry funding when public funding was unavailable. Under the herring program, a vessel notified NMFS of its intended trip and harvest. If NMFS required an observer without supplying a government-paid one, the vessel had to hire and pay a government-certified observer. NMFS estimated costs up to $710 per day and reductions of annual vessel-owner returns up to 20 percent. The fishermen disputed the agency’s statutory power to shift that expense to them; authorization to require an observer and authorization to make them pay were distinct propositions. (Printed 939–940.)
sections.Procedural History:
The Loper Bright businesses challenged the rule in February 2020 under the Magnuson-Stevens Act, which incorporated the APA. The district court entered summary judgment for the government, concluding that the statute authorized the rule and that Chevron would in any event support the agency if the text were ambiguous. A divided D.C. Circuit affirmed through Chevron’s second step after finding uncertainty about Congress’s answer. The Supreme Court considered whether to overrule Chevron. The packet’s note identifies the companion First Circuit case and Justice Jackson’s participation only in that case. (Printed 940, 961.)

Outside procedural supplement: the official opinion, 603 U.S. 369, 413, vacated the judgments of both the D.C. and First Circuits and remanded for proceedings consistent with the new interpretive rule. The Supreme Court did not itself decide that the statute ultimately forbade the observer-payment rule.
sections.Issue: Does APA § 706 permit courts to defer to an agency’s reasonable statutory interpretation merely because the statute is ambiguous? If Chevron conflicts with that provision, do stare decisis, agency expertise, political accountability, uniformity, or actual congressional delegations require retaining its framework? (Printed 943–953.)
sections.Holding: Chevron was overruled. Reviewing courts must use independent judgment to determine whether the statute authorizes the agency’s action. Agency interpretations may help persuade the court, and courts must honor actual statutory delegations of discretion within constitutional limits. Ambiguity alone does not require or permit Chevron-style deference under the APA. The holding rests on statutory grounds; Justice Thomas’s separate constitutional rationale is not the majority holding. Earlier holdings that particular agency actions were lawful remain subject to statutory stare decisis. (Printed 943–946, 952–953, 961–964.)
sections.Reasoning:
Chief Justice Roberts read § 706’s direction to decide legal questions and interpret constitutional and statutory provisions as adopting independent judicial interpretation. The majority contrasted that instruction with the APA’s express deferential standards for policy judgments and factfinding. Its historical account treated pre-APA respect for agency experience as consistent with courts’ responsibility to resolve law for themselves. It described Gray and Hearst as involving factbound applications within delegated responsibilities and disputed the dissent’s claim that they established a general rule like Chevron. (Printed 940–945.)

The majority rejected the premise that an unresolved statutory question necessarily delegates interpretive control to an agency. Ambiguity can arise from imprecision or from Congress’s failure to anticipate an issue. Courts regularly resolve such problems using interpretive tools. Technical subject matter can make agency assistance useful without transferring ultimate legal judgment. A wish for uniformity does not establish a preference for an incorrect interpretation, and the majority distinguished legal interpretation from policy choices that Congress actually entrusted to the agency. Courts must identify those delegations, fix their boundaries, and review the agency’s exercise of discretion for reasoned decisionmaking. (Printed 945–950.)

On stare decisis, the majority faulted Chevron’s failure to engage the APA, uncertainty about when language counted as ambiguous, proliferating threshold rules, inconsistent use, and the instability created by changes in administration. It preserved ordinary statutory stare decisis for earlier decisions upholding particular actions; reliance on Chevron alone was insufficient reason to overturn such a holding. (Printed 950–953.)

Justice Kagan’s dissent, joined by Justice Sotomayor and by Justice Jackson only for Relentless, disputed both the institutional premise and the statutory analysis. In her account, some statutes genuinely leave a range of choices, often involving expertise and policy. Congress would generally prefer the implementing agency to make those choices. Section 706 tells courts to decide legal questions but does not specify a de novo standard, and a court can decide a legal question by assessing an agency’s reasonableness. She relied on pre-APA and post-APA deference practices, Congress’s ability to amend the APA, and decades of reliance. She also argued that Skidmore respect and identifying actual delegations would themselves create difficult boundaries. (Printed 955–961.)

Justice Thomas separately argued that Chevron infringed Article III and improperly transferred judicial authority to the Executive. Justice Gorsuch emphasized independent judgment and distinguished historically respectful attention to consistent executive interpretations from an obligation to accept changing agency readings. Those concurrences supported the judgment while adding reasons beyond the Court’s statutory holding. (Printed 953–954.)

topics.lrs-i-independent-judgment: Loper Bright makes independent statutory interpretation the governing APA obligation in the course account.
topics.lrs-i-persuasive-weight: The majority retains Skidmore guidance and especially values consistent contemporaneous interpretations.
topics.lrs-i-delegated-discretion: The court must identify and honor actual discretionary delegations while policing their boundaries.
topics.lrs-i-statutory-stare-decisis: The majority preserves statutory stare decisis for earlier holdings despite changing methodology.
topics.lrs-i-law-fact: The competing readings of Gray and Hearst expose unresolved pressure on the law–fact distinction.
topics.lrs-i-historical-chevron: Loper Bright's account of Chevron's origins and erosion is the reference point for what the historical framework required.
